name: Creature of Habit Scale
developer: Ersche, Lim, Ward, Robbins and Stochl (2017)
construct: Individual differences in habitual tendencies in daily life: preference for routine and automatic, cue driven responding.
licence: Article statement: "This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)." The Cambridge repository copy is listed as Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives 4.0 International.
instructions: Not available as respondent facing text. Methods (Section 2.1): "Participants were required to indicate for each statement their level of agreement on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5)." The administered form in Appendix B is image only.

items.text: I tend to like routine.
I find comfort in regularity.
I rely on what is tried and tested rather than exploring something new.
I quite happily work within my comfort zone rather than challenging myself.
I tend to stick with the version of the software package that I am familiar with for as long as I can.
I generally cook with the same spices/flavourings.
I normally buy the same foods from the same grocery store.
In a restaurant, I tend to order dishes that I am familiar with.
I tend to do things in the same order every morning (e.g. get up, go to the bathroom, have a coffee…).
I always try to get the same seat in places such as on the bus, in the cinema, or in church.
I usually sit at the same place at the dinner table.
I like to park my car or bike always in the same place.
I always follow a certain order when preparing a meal.
I am one of those people who get really annoyed by last minute cancellations.
I tend to go to bed at roughly the same time every night.
I generally eat the same things for breakfast every day.
I often find myself finishing off a packet of biscuits just because it is lying there.
I often find myself opening up the cabinet to take a snack.
When walking past a plate of sweets or biscuits, I can't resist taking one.
Television makes me particularly prone to uncontrolled eating.
I often find myself eating without being aware of it.
I am prone to eating more when I feel stressed.
Eating crisps or biscuits straight out of the packet is typical of me.
Whenever I go into the kitchen, I typically look in the fridge.
I usually treat myself to a snack at the end of the workday.
I often take a snack while on the go (e.g. when driving, walking down the street, or surfing the web).
I often find myself running on 'autopilot', and then wonder why I ended up in a particular place or doing something that I did not intend to do.

subscales.name: Routine
subscales.description: Preference for routine and familiarity. Sum of the 16 Routine items.

subscales.name: Automaticity
subscales.description: Automatic, cue driven responding, largely food related. Sum of the 11 Automaticity items.

scoring: Score each subscale separately; higher scores indicate stronger routine preference or greater automaticity. The authors state that "individuals should be assessed on the basis of the score of each scale separately, rather than by an overall score of both scales" because the subscales correlate only weakly (r = 0.14). No reverse scored items remain in the final 27 item scale. No cut offs are published.
citation: Ersche, K. D., Lim, T.-V., Ward, L. H. E., Robbins, T. W., & Stochl, J. (2017). Creature of Habit: A self-report measure of habitual routines and automatic tendencies in everyday life. Personality and Individual Differences, 116, 73–85. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2017.04.024
transcriptionNote: Items transcribed from Table 2 of the PMC article (the final 27 item scale), listed in table order with Routine items first and Automaticity items second. The numbering 1 to 27 is assigned here for codebook convenience; the source identifies items by pool labels (COHS-n and COHSF-n), recorded in each item note. The administered questionnaire layout and respondent instructions in Appendix B are image only and could not be read, so the item order on the published form and the intermediate anchor labels (values 2 to 4) are not confirmed. The article names only the endpoints strongly disagree (1) and strongly agree (5).
